title: Volunteers Clean Máncora Beach
paragraphs: More than two hundred volunteers cleaned the beach in Máncora, in northern Peru, last Sunday. They collected almost three tonnes of rubbish in only four hours.

The event was organised by a group of university students from Piura. They shared the idea on social media two weeks earlier, and many surfers, local families and tourists joined. Everyone received gloves and large bags.

Most of the rubbish was plastic: bottles, bags and small pieces of fishing net. 'We found much more than we expected,' said student leader Ricardo Ato. 'But after four hours, the beach looked completely different.'

The tourist office gave free lunch to all the volunteers, and a local restaurant offered fish soup for just ten soles. The group is planning another clean-up in two months, and they want to bring a thousand people.
If you want to help, you can send a message to the group's page. Remember to bring a hat, sun cream and a water bottle.

title: Where Does Chocolate Come From?
paragraphs: Chocolate is one of the most popular foods in the world, but its history is very old. The first people to use cacao lived in Mexico and Central America more than three thousand years ago.

The Maya and the Aztecs didn't eat chocolate bars. They made a bitter drink from ground cacao beans, water and spices. This drink was often served at important ceremonies, and the beans were even used as money.

In the sixteenth century, Spanish explorers took cacao to Europe. At first, the drink was too bitter for them, so they added sugar and milk. Chocolate was soon enjoyed by rich families in Spain, France and England. The first solid chocolate bars were made only in the nineteenth century.
Today, most cacao is grown in West Africa, but countries like Ecuador, Peru and Mexico also produce excellent cacao. The best chocolate has a high percentage of cacao and very little sugar.
Next time you eat a piece of chocolate, remember: you are tasting a food with a history of three thousand years.

title: Three Months in Mendoza
paragraphs: Three months ago I moved from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a new job at a wine company. I'm twenty-six, and it's the first time I live away from my family. Here is what I love and what I miss.

What I love: Mendoza is calmer than Buenos Aires. I go to work by bike, and the journey takes only fifteen minutes. On weekends, I can see the Andes from the park, and the sunsets are beautiful. The rent is cheaper too: I pay 220,000 pesos for a small flat, and I have a balcony.

What I miss: my family and my friends, of course. I also miss the big bookshops and the cinemas of Buenos Aires. Here, there are fewer places to go at night. And I miss the food that my mum cooks on Sundays. I'm learning to cook, but my empanadas are terrible!
What surprised me: Many shops close from one to four in the afternoon. At first I was frustrated, but now I enjoy having a quiet lunch at home.
My advice for people who move to a new city: join a club or a class. Last month I joined a running group, and I made five new friends.

title: An Email to My Host Family
paragraphs: Dear Mr and Mrs Walker,
Thank you for your email. I'm very happy to stay with your family in Sydney for six weeks. Let me tell you a little about myself.

My name is Isabela Mejía, and I'm eighteen. I live in Bogotá with my parents and my younger brother. I'm finishing school this year, and I'm going to study tourism next year. I love music, and I play the piano every day. In my free time, I also like swimming and cooking.
I eat everything, except mushrooms. I'm not allergic to anything. I don't smoke, and I'm a tidy person. I can help in the kitchen, and I can wash the dishes after dinner.
My flight arrives at 6:45 a.m. on 12 January. I don't know the city, so could you tell me how to get to your house? I can take a taxi if it isn't too expensive. How much does it cost?
I have a few questions about the house. Is there wifi? Can I use the washing machine? And what is the weather like in January? I need to know what clothes to bring.
I'm very excited. See you soon!
Best wishes,
Isabela

title: The Wrong Address
paragraphs: Sebastián works as a delivery rider in Bogotá. One rainy Friday evening, he was riding his motorbike with a pizza for a customer called Nicolás. He arrived at the address, an old yellow house, and rang the bell.

A woman of about seventy opened the door. 'I didn't order a pizza,' she said. Sebastián checked his phone and saw his mistake: he was on Calle 45, but the address was Carrera 45. 'I'm sorry, señora,' he said. 'I'm going to leave right now.'

The woman looked at the pizza and smiled. 'Wait. Is it a mushroom pizza?' 'Yes.' 'It was my husband's favourite,' she said. 'He passed away last year, and I haven't eaten one since then.' Sebastián didn't know what to say.
He called the customer and explained the problem. Nicolás was very kind. 'Don't worry,' he said. 'Leave the pizza with that lady. I'll order another one.'

The woman paid for the pizza and invited Sebastián to come in for a coffee. They talked for twenty minutes about her husband's guitar and her garden. When Sebastián left, she gave him a big tip. 'Come back soon,' she said. 'Next time, bring a pizza on purpose!'

title: Three Days at Iguazú Falls
paragraphs: Thursday. We arrived at Puerto Iguazú by plane at nine in the morning. Our hostel is small but clean, and the owner gave us a map and some advice: 'Start early, and take a raincoat.' She was right on both things.

Friday. We entered the national park at eight, when it opened. We walked on narrow metal paths over the river, and we heard the noise of the falls before we saw them. At the end, we reached the Devil's Throat, the biggest waterfall. The water falls with so much power that everything around is wet. In five minutes, we were completely soaked, and we couldn't stop laughing.

Saturday. This morning we took a boat to a small island, and in the afternoon we saw a lot of animals: colourful butterflies, small monkeys and a coati, a small animal with a long nose. It tried to steal my sandwich!

Sunday. We went to the Brazilian side. The view there is wider, and you can see all the falls together. I took more than two hundred photos, but nothing is as beautiful as the real thing. Tomorrow we're flying home, and I'm already planning to come back.

title: Javiera and Her Phone Cases
focus: Present simple; future with going to
paragraphs: Javiera Soto is nineteen and studies graphic design in Concepción, Chile. Six months ago, she began to sell phone cases with her own drawings. Today she has more than six hundred followers online.
Interviewer: Where did the idea come from?
Javiera: I draw animals and plants in my notebooks. A friend said, 'These would look great on a phone case.' I ordered ten blank cases and printed my designs at the university.
Interviewer: How do you sell them?
Javiera: Mostly on social media. I post photos, and people send me a message. A case costs 8,000 pesos, and I send it by post in two days. Last month I sold forty cases.
Interviewer: What is the hardest part?
Javiera: Time and money. I have classes all day, so I only work at night. And I don't have a printer, so I pay for each print. If I earn more, I'm going to buy my own machine.
Interviewer: Do you have any advice?
Javiera: Start small, and don't be afraid to fail. My first designs were awful, but I learned from every mistake. If you wait until everything is perfect, you'll never start.

title: How to Use the Subte in Buenos Aires
paragraphs: The Buenos Aires underground, called the Subte, is one of the fastest ways to move around the city. It's easy to use if you follow these steps.
Step 1: Buy a card. You can buy a rechargeable card at a station, a kiosk or a shop. Ask for a card called SUBE. You don't need a new card every time: you add money to the same one.
Step 2: Add money. Use the machine at the station or an app. Put in enough money for several trips. If your card has no money, the gate doesn't open.

Step 3: Check your line. The Subte has six lines, and each one has a letter and a colour. Look at the map at the station and find your destination. Then look for the name of the last station on your line to know the direction.
Step 4: Go through the gate and wait behind the yellow line. Let people get off first, and then get on. If it's crowded, keep your bag in front of you.
Tip: Avoid rush hour, from eight to nine in the morning and from five to seven in the evening. If possible, travel a little earlier or later.

title: Free Wifi Arrives in Quito's Parks
focus: Passive voice; future with going to
paragraphs: The city of Quito has started a new project: free wifi in twenty public parks. The project was announced on Monday by the mayor, and it is available from today.

To use the network, people don't need a password. They only have to choose the network called 'Quito Libre' and accept the rules. The connection is fast enough to watch videos and make video calls, but each person has a limit of two hours a day.

The city spent about 150,000 dollars on the project. 'Many students don't have internet at home,' said the mayor. 'Now they can do their homework in a park instead of a café.' Some people were also worried about safety, so the parks have new lights and more police at night.

Not everyone agrees with the idea. A few neighbours think that people are going to spend too much time on their phones and stop talking to each other. 'In a park, you should look at the trees, not at the screen,' said one woman.
The city is going to ask people for their opinion in three months. If the project is successful, it will be extended to fifty more places next year.

title: Three Useful Inventions with a Latin American Link
paragraphs: We use many things every day without knowing where they come from. Here are three useful inventions with a connection to Latin America.

The ballpoint pen. In the 1930s, a Hungarian journalist called László Bíró worked for a newspaper in Hungary. He noticed that newspaper ink dried very fast, so he made a pen with a small ball at the end. The ball turned and put a thin line of ink on the paper. In the 1940s he moved to Argentina, and his pen was made there. His invention was soon used by pilots, and today millions of pens are sold every year.

The pacemaker. In 1958, a Colombian engineer called Jorge Reynolds Pombo built one of the first machines to help a sick heart. It was big and heavy and used a car battery. Today, pacemakers are very small and save thousands of lives.

The wristwatch. In 1904, the Brazilian pilot Alberto Santos-Dumont found it difficult to look at his pocket watch while flying. His friend Louis Cartier made him a watch that could be worn on the wrist. It was one of the first wristwatches for men. Soon, many people wanted one.
These inventions show that good ideas can come from anywhere. Often, they start with a simple problem and a person who wants to solve it.
